name: NetworkPolicy: control ingress
objective: CKS › Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities. Drill EVERY NetworkPolicy corner harder than the exam: default-deny ingress & egress, allow-by-pod-label, allow-by-namespace, the AND-vs-OR peer trap, port+protocol scoping, ipBlock with except, allow-DNS, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly on the policy spec, per requirement. (kindnet does not enforce policies, so grading is on the authored spec.)

questions.title: Default-deny-all ingress
questions.teach:
A **default-deny ingress** policy isolates every pod from inbound traffic. An empty `podSelector: {}` selects all pods in the namespace, and `policyTypes: [Ingress]` with **no** `ingress` rules denies all inbound.

**Gotcha:** list `Ingress` in `policyTypes` but add zero rules — any `ingress` block starts *allowing* traffic instead of denying it.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy `default-deny-ingress` that selects **all** pods and denies all ingress.

Target: empty `podSelector` ({}), `policyTypes: [Ingress]`, and zero ingress rules.
questions.hint: `spec.podSelector: {}`, `policyTypes: [Ingress]`, and omit the `ingress:` key entirely. Apply with `kubectl apply -f -`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
EOF

verification.description: default-deny-ingress: empty podSelector, Ingress type, no ingress rules

questions.eli5:
Imagine every pod is a house, and by default every house leaves its front door wide open — anyone on the street can walk in.

A **default-deny ingress** policy is like hiring a security guard who stands at the door of **every** house in the neighbourhood (`podSelector: {}` = all pods) and, by default, turns **everybody** away who wants to come *in*. That's it — no visitor list, so no visitors.

The trick is in *how* you say "turn everyone away". You tell Kubernetes two things:

- "This guard watches **incoming** people" (`policyTypes: [Ingress]`).
- Then you give the guard **no visitor list at all** (you leave out the `ingress:` section entirely).

A guard who is watching the door but has an empty guest list lets nobody in. Perfect lockdown.

Note this only affects people walking **in** (ingress). The houses can still send mail **out** (egress) freely — you haven't touched that.

**Watch out for:**

- **Writing `policyTypes: [Ingress]` but then adding an empty `ingress: []` or any `ingress:` rule.** The moment you add an ingress block, you stop denying and start *allowing* whatever that block describes. For a true default-deny, **omit the `ingress:` key completely**.
- **Egress is untouched.** This policy denies inbound only; outbound traffic still flows.
- **Policies only add allowances** — a later "allow" policy can poke holes in this deny. Default-deny is the floor you build allow-rules on top of.
- **Needs a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy** (Calico, Cilium, etc.). kindnet does *not* enforce it, so here you're graded on the written spec, not live blocking.
questions.deepDive:
## Default-deny ingress — full rundown

### Mental model
NetworkPolicy is **additive and allowlist-based**. With **no** policy, all pods accept all traffic. The *instant* a policy's `podSelector` selects a pod for a given direction, that pod flips to **default-deny for that direction** — and from then on only what some policy explicitly *allows* gets through. A default-deny policy is simply a policy that selects pods for a direction but allows **nothing**, locking them down so you can add precise allow-rules on top.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector: {}        # {} = every pod in this namespace
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress              # govern the INBOUND direction
  # NO ingress: key  ->  zero allow rules  ->  deny all inbound
```

### Why each field matters
| Field | Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `podSelector` | `{}` (empty) | Selects **all** pods in the namespace |
| `podSelector` | `matchLabels: {app: web}` | Selects only matching pods |
| `policyTypes` | `[Ingress]` | This policy governs inbound only |
| `ingress:` | *absent* | No allow rules → all inbound denied |
| `ingress: []` | empty list | **Also** denies all (but be deliberate) |

### Empty-selector cheatsheet
| Where `{}` appears | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `spec.podSelector: {}` | all pods in the namespace |
| `from: [{podSelector: {}}]` | all pods in **this** namespace (as sources) |
| `from: [{namespaceSelector: {}}]` | all pods in **all** namespaces |
| `from: []` or omitted | **no** sources → denies (default-deny) |

That last row is the crux: an **omitted** `from`/`ingress` denies, while an **empty `{}` selector** means "everything".

### policyTypes nuance
If you omit `policyTypes`, Kubernetes infers it from which rule blocks are present — but it will **only** include `Egress` if you wrote an `egress:` block. For a default-deny you have *no* rule block, so you **must** list `policyTypes` explicitly or nothing is governed. Always set it.

### Namespace scope
A NetworkPolicy is **namespaced**. `default-deny-ingress` in `netpol-learn` only affects pods in `netpol-learn`. To lock down the whole cluster you apply one default-deny per namespace.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol default-deny-ingress -o yaml
kubectl -n netpol-learn describe netpol default-deny-ingress
# Spec.Ingress should show "<none>" or no rules
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Adding any `ingress:` block turns deny into allow.** `ingress: - {}` means "allow from everyone" — the exact opposite. Omit the key.
- **`policyTypes` is mandatory here** — without a rule block, omitting it leaves the direction ungoverned.
- **Ingress-only.** Egress still flows; add a separate default-deny-egress if you need both. A combined deny uses `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` with no rule blocks.
- **Additive, never subtractive.** This policy sets the floor; other policies can only *add* allowed paths, never tighten this one.
- **Pod-local flip.** Only pods matched by *some* policy's `podSelector` go default-deny; unselected pods stay wide open.
- **Enforcement needs a policy-aware CNI** (Calico, Cilium, Weave, Antrea). Flannel/kindnet ignore policies — they are stored but never enforced.

### Quick reference
```yaml
# Deny all inbound to every pod in the namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
# (no ingress: rules)
```
```bash
kubectl -n netpol-learn apply -f deny.yaml
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol
```

questions.title: Allow ingress from a specific pod label
questions.teach:
To let specific source pods in, add an `ingress` rule whose `from` entry is a **`podSelector`** matching their labels. A `from` `podSelector` matches source pods **in the policy's own namespace**.

**Gotcha:** `podSelector: {}` inside `from` means *all pods in this namespace*, but an empty `from: []` matches **no** sources at all.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy `allow-from-client` that selects pods labelled `app=web` and allows ingress **only** from pods labelled `role=client`.

Target: `spec.podSelector` matches `app=web`; one ingress rule with a single `from` entry whose `podSelector` matches `role=client`.
questions.hint: `spec.podSelector.matchLabels.app: web`, then `ingress: [{ from: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: client } } }] }]`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-client
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          role: client
EOF

verification.description: allow-from-client: targets app=web, allows from podSelector role=client

questions.eli5:
Think of your `app=web` pods as a members-only club, and the club already has a strict door policy: nobody gets in unless they're on a list.

An **ingress `from` podSelector** is you handing the bouncer a list that says: *"only let in people wearing a `role=client` badge."* Anyone with that badge walks in; everyone else is turned away.

In Kubernetes terms:

- `spec.podSelector: {app: web}` = *which* pods this door policy protects (the club).
- `ingress.from[].podSelector: {role=client}` = *who* is on the guest list (the allowed source pods).

One important detail about the guest list: it only knows people **from the same building** (the same namespace). A `from` `podSelector` on its own matches source pods in the policy's **own** namespace — it won't recognise a `role=client` badge worn by someone in a different namespace.

**Watch out for:**

- **`podSelector: {}` inside `from` means *everyone in this namespace*** — an empty selector matches all pods, not none. That's very different from...
- **An empty `from: []` (or omitting `from`), which matches *no* sources** — so it denies everything for that rule. Empty-selector vs empty-list is the classic trap.
- **A `from` `podSelector` is namespace-local.** To allow clients from another namespace you need a `namespaceSelector` too (a later lesson).
- **Labels must match exactly** — `role=client` ≠ `role=Client`. One typo and the bouncer lets nobody in.
- **This is additive.** Selecting `app=web` flips those pods to default-deny inbound, and this rule only *adds back* the `role=client` path. Everyone else stays blocked.
questions.deepDive:
## Allow ingress from a pod label — full rundown

### Mental model
Selecting a pod with a policy flips it to **default-deny** for that direction; each `ingress` rule then *adds back* a permitted source. A `from` **`podSelector`** names the allowed source pods **by label, within the policy's own namespace**. It answers "who may connect *in*?", while `spec.podSelector` answers "connect in *to whom*?".

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-client
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:              # the TARGET pods (destinations)
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:                   # the allowed SOURCES
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          role: client
```

### Two selectors, two jobs
| Selector | Location | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `spec.podSelector` | top of spec | Which pods does this policy protect? |
| `ingress[].from[].podSelector` | inside a `from` entry | Which source pods may connect in? |

### Namespace scope — critical
A `from` `podSelector` **by itself** only matches source pods in the **same namespace** as the policy. It does **not** reach into other namespaces. To allow a `role=client` pod living in namespace `foo`, you must add a `namespaceSelector` to the peer (see the AND/OR lesson).

### Empty-selector traps
| Written as | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `from: [{podSelector: {}}]` | **all** pods in this namespace |
| `from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {role: client}}}]` | only `role=client` pods here |
| `from: []` | **no** sources → nothing allowed (deny) |
| *(no `from:` in the rule)* | the rule allows **all** sources on any listed ports |

`{}` = everything; empty list / omitted-with-no-peers = nothing. These are opposites.

### matchLabels vs matchExpressions
```yaml
podSelector:
  matchExpressions:
  - key: role
    operator: In
    values: [client, admin]
```
`matchLabels` is exact equality (AND'd). `matchExpressions` supports `In`, `NotIn`, `Exists`, `DoesNotExist` for set-based matching. Both may appear; all conditions are AND'd.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n netpol-learn describe netpol allow-from-client
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol allow-from-client -o jsonpath='{.spec.ingress[0].from}'; echo
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`from` podSelector is namespace-scoped.** Clients in another namespace are NOT matched without a `namespaceSelector`.
- **`podSelector: {}` means all pods**, not zero — the opposite of an empty `from: []`.
- **Label typos silently block.** `role=client` ≠ `role=Client`; the API won't warn you.
- **Additive:** selecting `app=web` denies all other inbound; this rule only reopens the `role=client` path. Combine with a default-deny (or rely on the implicit flip) for full lockdown of everything else.
- **No `ports`?** The rule allows the source on **all** ports. Add `ports` to scope it (next lesson).
- **Enforcement requires a policy-aware CNI**; kindnet stores but does not enforce.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }   # target
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: client } }   # allowed source (same ns)
```

questions.title: Allow ingress from a namespace, on one port
questions.teach:
A `from` entry with a **`namespaceSelector`** admits every pod in any namespace matching that selector. Kubernetes auto-labels each namespace `kubernetes.io/metadata.name=<name>`. Add `ports` to the same rule to restrict which port the traffic may hit.

**Gotcha:** `namespaceSelector` matches namespace **labels**, not the name directly — and `{}` means *all* namespaces.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy `allow-from-monitoring` that selects pods labelled `app=web` and allows ingress from **any** pod in namespace `monitoring`, but **only** on TCP port `80`.

Target: `podSelector` app=web; an ingress rule with a `from` `namespaceSelector` matching `kubernetes.io/metadata.name=monitoring` AND `ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 80}]`.
questions.hint: `from: [{ namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring } } }]` plus `ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 80 }]` in the SAME ingress rule.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-monitoring
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
EOF

verification.description: allow-from-monitoring: from namespaceSelector name=monitoring, port TCP/80

questions.eli5:
Imagine your `app=web` pods are an office, and you want to let in **everyone who works in the Monitoring building** — but you don't know each person's name badge, you just know they come from that building. And you only want them to use **one specific door** (port 80).

A **`namespaceSelector`** is the rule: *"let in anybody whose building is tagged 'monitoring'."* It doesn't care about individual people (pods) — it admits the whole building.

How does Kubernetes know which building is "monitoring"? Every namespace automatically gets a nameplate label: `kubernetes.io/metadata.name=<its name>`. So you match on that label, and you've selected the `monitoring` namespace.

Adding **`ports`** to the same rule is like saying *"...and they may only use door 80, nothing else."* Traffic to any other port is still turned away.

**Watch out for:**

- **`namespaceSelector` matches namespace *labels*, not the name text.** You match the auto-label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring` — you can't just type the namespace name somewhere and expect it to work.
- **An empty `namespaceSelector: {}` means *ALL namespaces*** — a wide-open door. Always include the matchLabels unless you truly mean everywhere.
- **`namespaceSelector` admits *every* pod in that namespace.** To narrow it to specific pods in that namespace, you'd add a `podSelector` in the **same** peer entry (the AND trap, next lesson).
- **`ports` in the same rule scopes it.** Put the `ports` under the same `from` rule; no `ports` means all ports are allowed from that source.
- **Still additive** — this only *adds* the monitoring+port-80 path. It needs a default-deny (or the automatic deny-flip from selecting `app=web`) underneath for the restriction to mean anything.
questions.deepDive:
## Allow ingress from a namespace, on one port — full rundown

### Mental model
A `from` **`namespaceSelector`** admits traffic from **every pod in any namespace whose labels match** — it selects by namespace, not by individual pod. Pair it with **`ports`** in the same rule to restrict *which* port the admitted traffic may reach. Think: "which buildings may enter, and through which door".

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-monitoring
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring   # the auto-label
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
```

### The auto-label every namespace carries
Since Kubernetes 1.21, the apiserver (via the `NamespaceDefaultLabelName` admission) stamps every namespace with:
```
kubernetes.io/metadata.name: <namespace-name>
```
So `namespaceSelector` matching `kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring` targets the `monitoring` namespace **without** you having to add any label yourself. You may also use custom labels (`team: obs`) if you label the namespace.

### namespaceSelector matrix
| Written as | Matches |
|---|---|
| `namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring}}` | pods in ns `monitoring` |
| `namespaceSelector: {}` | pods in **all** namespaces |
| `namespaceSelector` + `podSelector` in **same** entry | AND — matching pods in matching ns |
| *(no `namespaceSelector`, just `podSelector`)* | pods in the **policy's own** namespace |

### The `ports` block
```yaml
ports:
- protocol: TCP      # TCP | UDP | SCTP; defaults to TCP if omitted
  port: 80           # numeric, or a named containerPort
  # endPort: 90      # optional range end (port..endPort), needs CNI support
```
- `ports` applies to the **whole** `from` list in that rule.
- No `ports` → all ports allowed from those sources.
- A rule with `ports` but empty `from` → those ports open to **all** sources.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl get ns monitoring --show-labels
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol allow-from-monitoring -o yaml
kubectl -n netpol-learn describe netpol allow-from-monitoring   # shows From: NamespaceSelector + Ports
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`namespaceSelector` matches namespace *labels*, not the name string.** Use the `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` auto-label (or a custom label), never a bare name field.
- **Empty `namespaceSelector: {}` = ALL namespaces** — a common accidental wide-open.
- **namespaceSelector admits every pod in the namespace.** To require a specific pod *and* a specific namespace, put `podSelector` and `namespaceSelector` in the **same** peer entry (AND, next lesson). As **separate** list items they become OR.
- **`protocol` defaults to TCP** if omitted; still, write it explicitly on the exam.
- **`ports` scopes the whole rule** — forgetting it leaves every port open to the namespace.
- **Additive** — needs an underlying default-deny (or the deny-flip from selecting `app=web`) for the "only port 80 from monitoring" restriction to actually bite.
- **CNI enforcement required**; kindnet does not enforce.

### Quick reference
```yaml
ingress:
- from:
  - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring } }
  ports:
  - { protocol: TCP, port: 80 }
```

questions.title: The AND-vs-OR peer trap
questions.teach:
Inside one `from`/`to` list, **separate entries are OR'd**, but `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` written as **keys of the same entry** are **AND'd** — both must match the source pod. This is the single most-tested NetworkPolicy gotcha.

**Gotcha:** two list items (`- namespaceSelector` then `- podSelector`) means *this namespace OR that pod*; combine them under ONE `- ` to require both.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy `allow-and` selecting pods labelled `app=web`, allowing ingress **only** from pods that are BOTH labelled `role=client` AND live in namespace `monitoring` (one combined peer).

Target: a single ingress `from` entry containing BOTH a `namespaceSelector` (name=monitoring) and a `podSelector` (role=client) — AND semantics, one list item.
questions.hint: ONE `from` list entry with two keys: `- namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring}}` and on the same item `podSelector: {matchLabels: {role: client}}`. Not two separate `- ` items.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-and
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          role: client
EOF

verification.description: allow-and: ONE from entry with BOTH namespaceSelector(monitoring) AND podSelector(role=client)

questions.eli5:
This is the single trickiest NetworkPolicy idea, and it's all about **indentation**.

Picture the bouncer's guest list. You want to admit only people who are **BOTH** wearing a `role=client` badge **AND** arriving from the `monitoring` building. Both conditions, same person.

Here's the trap. In YAML, a `from` list can have several entries, each starting with a dash `-`:

- If you write **two separate dashed items** — one `- namespaceSelector` and one `- podSelector` — Kubernetes reads them as **two independent guests**: "anyone from monitoring, **OR** anyone with a client badge." Way too permissive!
- If you write **one dashed item with both keys inside it**, Kubernetes reads it as **one guest who must satisfy both**: "from monitoring **AND** wearing a client badge." That's what you want.

So the rule is:

- **Different list items (each with its own `-`) = OR.**
- **Multiple selectors under the *same* `-` item = AND.**

Same person vs. two people. The dash is everything.

**Watch out for:**

- **Two `- ` items = OR, not AND.** Writing `- namespaceSelector` then `- podSelector` as separate items lets in *monitoring OR client* — far wider than intended.
- **To get AND, both selectors go under ONE `- ` entry**, with the second key (`podSelector`) indented to align with `namespaceSelector`, no extra dash.
- **This only applies within a single peer entry.** The OR-across-entries / AND-within-entry rule is the exam's favourite gotcha.
- **A `namespaceSelector` without a `podSelector` in the same entry** means *all pods* in that namespace — the `podSelector` is what narrows it to `role=client`.
- **Indentation errors are silent-ish:** the policy still applies, just with the wrong (looser) meaning. Always re-read the YAML structure.
questions.deepDive:
## The AND-vs-OR peer trap — full rundown

### Mental model
Inside a single `from` (or `to`) list:
- **Separate list items are OR'd** — traffic matching *any* entry is allowed.
- **`namespaceSelector` + `podSelector` written as keys of the *same* entry are AND'd** — the source must satisfy *both*.

This hinges entirely on YAML structure: one `-` (dash) starts one peer entry. This is the most-tested NetworkPolicy gotcha on the CKS.

### AND — one peer entry (what we want)
```yaml
ingress:
- from:
  - namespaceSelector:                         # \
      matchLabels:                              #  } ONE list entry
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring #  } both keys AND'd
    podSelector:                                #  } note: no leading "-"
      matchLabels:                              # /
        role: client
```
Meaning: **pods labelled `role=client` that live in namespace `monitoring`.** Both must be true.

### OR — two peer entries (the trap)
```yaml
ingress:
- from:
  - namespaceSelector:                          # entry #1
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring
  - podSelector:                                # entry #2  (extra "-"!)
      matchLabels:
        role: client
```
Meaning: **any pod in `monitoring` (any label), OR any `role=client` pod in the policy's own namespace.** Much wider — usually wrong.

### Side-by-side
| YAML structure | Semantics | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| `- namespaceSelector:` … newline … `  podSelector:` (same item) | **AND** | client pods *in* monitoring |
| `- namespaceSelector:` … `- podSelector:` (two items) | **OR** | all of monitoring *or* all clients here |

The visual tell: count the dashes under `from:`. **One dash = AND. Two dashes = OR.**

### Why it matters for security
OR is almost always too permissive. "Allow from monitoring namespace OR from any client pod" opens the target to every pod in monitoring *regardless of label* and to client pods anywhere the selector reaches. AND enforces true least privilege: a specific identity in a specific location.

### The four peer types (any combine within one entry = AND)
| Peer key | Selects by |
|---|---|
| `podSelector` | pod labels (own ns, unless paired with namespaceSelector) |
| `namespaceSelector` | namespace labels |
| `podSelector` + `namespaceSelector` (same entry) | AND: matching pods in matching namespaces |
| `ipBlock` | CIDR (cannot be combined with the selectors in one entry) |

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol allow-and -o yaml
# Confirm spec.ingress[0].from has ONE element with BOTH keys:
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol allow-and \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.ingress[0].from[0]}'; echo
```
If that one element shows both `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector`, it's AND. If `from` has two elements, it's OR.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Two `- ` entries = OR**, not AND — the headline trap. The extra dash silently loosens the policy.
- **AND = both selectors under one `- ` entry**, with `podSelector` indented to the same column as `namespaceSelector` (no dash).
- **`ipBlock` can't share an entry with podSelector/namespaceSelector** — it's its own peer type.
- **A namespaceSelector alone in the AND entry still means "all pods in that ns"** — it's the paired podSelector that narrows to `role=client`.
- **Bad indentation doesn't error**; it just changes the meaning. Re-read the structure before submitting.
- **Enforcement needs a policy-aware CNI**; kindnet stores but does not enforce.

### Quick reference
```yaml
# AND: role=client pods located in the monitoring namespace
from:
- namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring } }
  podSelector:       { matchLabels: { role: client } }
```

questions.title: Allow ingress from a CIDR, with an exception
questions.teach:
An `ipBlock` peer admits traffic by **CIDR** (for external or node IPs that have no pod labels). `cidr` sets the allowed range and `except` carves out sub-ranges to deny inside it.

**Gotcha:** every entry in `except` must be **within** the `cidr` range, or the API rejects the policy.
questions.prompt:
In `netpol-learn`, create a NetworkPolicy `allow-from-cidr` selecting pods labelled `app=web`, allowing ingress from CIDR `10.0.0.0/16` **except** `10.0.5.0/24`.

Target: `podSelector` app=web; one ingress `from` entry with `ipBlock.cidr=10.0.0.0/16` and `ipBlock.except=[10.0.5.0/24]`.
questions.hint: `from: [{ ipBlock: { cidr: 10.0.0.0/16, except: [10.0.5.0/24] } }]`. The except CIDR must sit inside the main cidr.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-cidr
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.0/16
        except:
        - 10.0.5.0/24
EOF
questions.eli5:
Sometimes the thing you want to let in isn't a pod at all — it's a plain IP address. Maybe it's an external office, a VPN range, or a load balancer. Those don't wear Kubernetes labels, so pod/namespace selectors can't see them. For those, you match on **IP range** instead.

An **`ipBlock`** is like telling the bouncer: *"let in anyone whose home address is on Maple Street"* — a whole street (a CIDR range like `10.0.0.0/16`).

The **`except`** part is the twist: *"...except houses 10.0.5.0 through 10.0.5.255 on that street — those stay out."* You allow the big range, then carve out a smaller block inside it to deny.

So `cidr: 10.0.0.0/16` opens the whole neighbourhood, and `except: [10.0.5.0/24]` punches a "not these" hole inside it.

**Watch out for:**

- **Every `except` range must sit *inside* the main `cidr`.** If you put an `except` that isn't a sub-range of the cidr, the API **rejects** the whole policy. `10.0.5.0/24` is inside `10.0.0.0/16` — good. `192.168.0.0/24` would not be — rejected.
- **`ipBlock` is for IPs, not pods.** Use it for external/node IPs that have no labels; use `podSelector`/`namespaceSelector` for in-cluster pods.
- **`ipBlock` can't be combined with pod/namespace selectors in the same `- ` entry** — it stands alone as its own peer.
- **Pod IPs are ephemeral.** Matching in-cluster pods by IP is brittle; prefer label selectors for pods and reserve `ipBlock` for truly external ranges.
- **Still additive** — this only adds the allowed CIDR path; the deny-flip from selecting `app=web` keeps everyone else out.
questions.deepDive:
## Allow ingress from a CIDR with an exception — full rundown

### Mental model
Pod and namespace selectors match **labelled in-cluster objects**. An **`ipBlock`** peer matches by **IP CIDR** instead — the escape hatch for traffic that has no pod/namespace identity: external clients, VPN ranges, node IPs, load balancers. `cidr` opens a range; `except` carves denied sub-ranges out of it.

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-cidr
  namespace: netpol-learn
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.0/16        # allowed range
        except:
        - 10.0.5.0/24            # denied sub-range INSIDE the cidr
```

### How cidr + except resolve
| Source IP | In `10.0.0.0/16`? | In `except 10.0.5.0/24`? | Allowed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `10.0.1.7` | yes | no | ✅ |
| `10.0.5.42` | yes | yes | ❌ |
| `10.1.0.9` | no | — | ❌ (outside cidr) |
| `192.168.1.1` | no | — | ❌ |

`except` subtracts from `cidr`; everything outside `cidr` is denied anyway (additive model).

### The hard rule on `except`
Every `except` CIDR **must be a strict subset of** `cidr`, or the apiserver rejects the policy:
```
spec.ingress[0].from[0].ipBlock.except[0]: Invalid value:
"192.168.0.0/24": not within CIDR "10.0.0.0/16"
```
So `10.0.5.0/24 ⊂ 10.0.0.0/16` is valid; an unrelated range is not.

### ipBlock standalone rule
`ipBlock` is its **own** peer type and **cannot** be combined with `podSelector`/`namespaceSelector` in the **same** `from` entry:
```yaml
# WRONG — ipBlock alongside a selector in one entry is rejected
- ipBlock: { cidr: 10.0.0.0/16 }
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: client } }   # invalid

# RIGHT — separate entries (OR)
- ipBlock: { cidr: 10.0.0.0/16 }
- podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: client } }
```

### Pod IPs & ipBlock caveats
- Some CNIs **SNAT** traffic, so the source IP the policy sees may be the node IP, not the original client — `ipBlock` matching can behave unexpectedly across CNIs.
- Pod IPs are **ephemeral**; never pin in-cluster pods by IP. Use label selectors for pods; reserve `ipBlock` for external/stable ranges.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol allow-from-cidr -o yaml
kubectl -n netpol-learn get netpol allow-from-cidr \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.ingress[0].from[0].ipBlock}'; echo
# dry-run to catch an out-of-range except before applying
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f policy.yaml
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`except` must be within `cidr`** or the policy is rejected by the API server.
- **`ipBlock` cannot share a `from` entry** with pod/namespace selectors.
- **ipBlock matches IPs, not labels** — wrong tool for in-cluster pods.
- **SNAT/CNI behaviour** can rewrite the observed source IP; test against your actual CNI.
- **Additive** — only adds the allowed CIDR; the deny-flip from `app=web` keeps all other sources out.
- **Enforcement requires a policy-aware CNI**; kindnet does not enforce.

### Quick reference
```yaml
ingress:
- from:
  - ipBlock:
      cidr: 10.0.0.0/16
      except: [10.0.5.0/24]   # must be inside the cidr
```
